rules.statement: Don't report a void helper that only adds failures to a list the caller passes as a command-query separation violation; the rule forbids a method that both acts and answers.
rules.why: A void command that only appends results answers nothing, so it doesn't mix acting and answering. Sibling helpers in the same validator often have the same shape.
rules.check: Before reporting, see whether the helper also returns a value or answers a query. If it is void and only mutates the passed collection, and its sibling helpers do the same, don't raise it.

rules.statement: Don't ask for CultureInfo.InvariantCulture when numbers are interpolated into exception messages meant for people; the invariant-culture rule covers values meant for machines.
rules.why: The convention asks for the invariant culture on machine-read values. Exception messages are for people, and an integer such as a long formats with no group separators in any culture.
rules.check: Before reporting, check whether the formatted text is read by a machine (a request path, a protocol value, a persisted value) or only by a person (an exception or log message). Report only the machine case.

rules.statement: Don't ask for a trailing newline on test fixture files that are stored byte for byte as an external service served them.
rules.why: Such fixtures are captured documents that are never edited. Adding an LF would make them differ from what the service serves.
rules.check: Before reporting a missing trailing LF on a fixture, check the fixtures README or the repository conventions for a byte-exact or never-edited rule.

rules.statement: Don't report a chain of member accesses on one receiver as a nested-call violation; the no-nested-call rule covers only a call nested in another call's arguments.
rules.why: The rule asks you to hoist call results that are passed as arguments into named locals. No rule covers a fluent chain such as a.B.Get<T>(x).Value.ToArray().
rules.check: Raise it only when a method call appears inside another call's argument list, including constructor arguments and lambda bodies. Don't raise a plain member-access chain.

rules.statement: Before reporting that a test name doesn't match a test-data builder's setting, check how the builder derives the named count from that setting.
rules.why: Test names may count what the builder produces (for example, setting + 1), or count from the point the code under test starts, rather than echo the raw setting. In that case the name is accurate.
rules.check: Read the builder's defaults and derived properties, and the sibling test that pins the other side of the limit, before raising a name/setting mismatch.

rules.statement: In a test project, test that cancelling the caller's token surfaces an OperationCanceledException and not a wrapped domain exception.
rules.why: Without this test, a regression could turn host shutdown into a domain error that is logged as an outage.
rules.check: For each async component that translates exceptions, look for a test that passes a cancelled token and asserts ThrowsAnyAsync<OperationCanceledException>.

rules.statement: In a test project, pin each inclusive or exclusive limit with one case exactly at the limit and one case just past it.
rules.why: If no test sits on the limit, flipping >= to > or making an off-by-one change leaves the suite green.
rules.check: For each comparison against a limit in the code under test, look for a case at the exact value and one a tick or unit beyond it.

rules.statement: In a test project, give every validation failure branch its own test that asserts the failure message with an ordinal comparison.
rules.why: If a guard has no test, it can be removed or its message changed without any test failing.
rules.check: Map each failure message in a validator to a test that triggers it and asserts the message text.

rules.statement: In a test project, test that a cache doesn't keep a failed fetch: the next call after a failure fetches again and succeeds.
rules.why: If a failure were cached, a transient outage would persist until restart with no failing test.
rules.check: For caching components, look for a test where the first fetch fails, the second succeeds, and two requests are recorded.

rules.statement: In a test project, cover every public overload, including Action<TOptions> configure overloads, with a test that asserts its effect.
rules.why: Without that test, a regression such as an overload not applying its delegate would go unnoticed.
rules.check: List the public overloads that a diff adds and look for a test that calls each one.

rules.statement: In a test project, assert a message substring that is unique to the rule under test, not text that several failure paths share.
rules.why: If two tests assert the same shared substring, each passes when the other path refuses, so neither pins its own rule.
rules.check: Compare the asserted substrings of sibling failure tests with the messages each path produces.

rules.statement: In a test project, for each registration method that calls ValidateOnStart, add a test that starts a host with invalid options and asserts an OptionsValidationException that names the key.
rules.why: Tests that only call Validate directly would stay green if ValidateOnStart were dropped from a registration path.
rules.check: For each AddX registration that validates on start, look for a host-start test with an invalid value.

rules.statement: In a test project, move test wiring and assertion helpers that several test classes duplicate into shared test infrastructure.
rules.why: Copies of wiring have to be changed twice and can drift apart.
rules.check: Look for identical setup, dispose loops or assertion helpers copied between test classes.

rules.statement: Extract repeated validation or exception-translation blocks that differ only by a name or parameter into one shared helper.
rules.why: Copies can drift, and two components would then report different errors for the same failure.
rules.check: Look for near-identical try/catch or catch-filter blocks repeated within a class or across sibling classes.

rules.statement: Don't pass two parameters that identify the same entity (such as a name and an index); pass one and derive the other from it.
rules.why: A long positional list of similar values is easy to misorder, and the values can disagree.
rules.check: Look for method signatures in a diff that gain a parameter redundant with an existing one.

rules.statement: Register services with TryAdd* unconditionally, and don't use an Any() guard with an early return that skips registering other services.
rules.why: If something else registers the guarded service first, the early return silently leaves the dependent services unregistered.
rules.check: Look for services.Any(...) checks followed by AddSingleton or a return in DI extension methods.

rules.statement: Keep measured or volatile external figures (rates, cadences, dates of observed state) out of ADR Consequences and XML docs, or date them; state the rationale and keep the dated figures in the ADR's Context.
rules.why: Undated figures go stale unnoticed, and readers may tune limits on the old numbers.
rules.check: Look for numeric cadences, estimates or observed-state claims in XML docs, READMEs or ADR Consequences without an 'as of <date>' qualifier.

rules.statement: Give a documented method a <param> tag for each parameter, and a <returns> tag when it returns a value.
rules.why: Without them, IntelliSense describes none of the parameters.
rules.check: Look for /// summaries on methods that lack <param> or <returns> tags.

rules.statement: In production code, write transient buffers that are used once, such as hash outputs and decoded data, into stackalloc spans or ArrayPool<byte>.Shared buffers through the Try/destination overloads, not into newly allocated arrays.
rules.why: The allocating overloads add avoidable allocations on each call, which matters for large inputs.
rules.check: Look for HashData(x) and Convert.FromBase64String results that are used once and discarded on hot or per-request paths.
